readings.title: An invitation understood in different ways
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A community centre invited neighbours to a shared meal. Some believed they had to bring food, while others thought everything would be provided. The main obstacle was an invitation with an unclear request. The phrase bring something if you can did not say whether attendance depended on a contribution. At first, the people involved did not agree on which part of the proposal deserved the most attention.

To investigate, the team used a review of questions from invited families. Organizers asked what visitors had understood and which words made them hesitate. The organizers kept the first stage small enough to change without wasting substantial time or resources.

The evidence indicated a clear optional note encouraged attendance. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced an invitation stating that all were welcome without food. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. The records were useful because they described ordinary use rather than an ideal situation imagined at a meeting.

The case suggests a broader point: welcoming language must remove uncertainty. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. The group published its reasons so that people who preferred a different result could still understand the choice. For those taking part in an invitation understood in different ways, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records.

readings.title: Translating a safety announcement
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A sports centre printed a safety notice in several languages. One translated version used a formal term unfamiliar to most visitors. The main obstacle was a technically correct but confusing phrase. Readers could identify each word yet still could not tell where to leave equipment. The question mattered to people with different schedules and levels of experience, so one account could not represent everyone.

To investigate, the team used a practical reading exercise. Bilingual volunteers checked the intended action with readers while staff reviewed the final wording. A simple record of what happened each day gave the team a starting point for comparison.

The evidence indicated plain instructions worked across languages. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced revised notices checked by community readers. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. Some participants welcomed the change immediately, while others noticed practical details that needed further work.

The case suggests a broader point: translation quality depends on useful meaning. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. The result was a revised plan, not a claim that every difficulty had disappeared. For those taking part in translating a safety announcement, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: A festival timetable for newcomers
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A local festival attracted residents new to the town. The printed timetable named familiar places without addresses or transport information. The main obstacle was assumptions about local knowledge. People who had lived nearby for years knew the venues, but newcomers could not locate them. The initial idea sounded reasonable, yet the details of the place made it harder to carry out than expected.

To investigate, the team used a route check with first-time visitors. Volunteers asked people to find two events using only the published leaflet. Instead of relying on a single opinion, the team invited several users to describe what they actually did.

The evidence indicated landmarks and addresses improved navigation. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced a timetable with maps and transport notes. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. This allowed the organizers to separate a temporary inconvenience from a pattern that required attention.

The case suggests a broader point: public events should not require insider knowledge. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. They also decided when to check the arrangement again, because conditions could change over time. For those taking part in a festival timetable for newcomers, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: Speaking turns in a discussion group
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A neighbourhood discussion brought together people with different language backgrounds. Several participants had ideas but struggled to enter fast conversations. The main obstacle was a meeting pace that excluded slower speakers. The chair moved to new topics before everyone had time to respond. The people affected were invited to comment before a permanent arrangement was chosen.

To investigate, the team used a trial of short written reflection periods. Facilitators counted participation and invited anonymous comments on the format. The first trial produced both useful results and questions the team could not yet answer.

The evidence indicated brief pauses broadened the discussion. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced structured turns and a written option for comments. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. Rather than hide those limits, the public note explained how the next version had been selected.

The case suggests a broader point: good exchange makes room for different speaking styles. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. That explanation made later changes easier to discuss with residents and staff. For those taking part in speaking turns in a discussion group, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

translation.stem:
Translate the following passage into Chinese:
A useful plan for cross-cultural communication and community events must take account of the people who will use it. An idea may look complete on paper and still create difficulties during an ordinary week. Organizers therefore tried the community exchange programme on a small scale and invited comments from users with different schedules. They recorded benefits as well as the time and resources needed to provide them. Some findings supported the original aim, while others suggested that the method should change. The group published both kinds of result instead of presenting the trial as a simple success or failure. This allowed residents to discuss the next step with a clearer understanding of its possible effects.
translation.explanation: 参考译文供考生自评，注意语义准确、逻辑关系及汉语通顺。
translation.referenceAnswer: 关于跨文化交流与社区活动的有用方案必须考虑实际使用它的人。一个想法在纸上看似完整，平常使用时却仍可能出现困难。因此，组织者小规模试行该服务，并邀请时间安排不同的使用者提出意见。他们既记录益处，也记录提供这些益处所需的时间和资源。有些发现支持最初目标，另一些则表明方法应当调整。团队同时公布两类结果，而没有把试行简单说成成功或失败。这让居民能更清楚地了解可能的影响，再讨论下一步。

writing.stem: Write at least 100 words in English to the intercultural learning team about a community activity related to cross-cultural communication and community events. Explain how different people can participate, what should be recorded, and how the results should be shared.
writing.explanation: 范文供考生自评，注意任务要点、组织结构及语言准确性。
writing.sampleAnswer:
Dear Committee Members,
I would like to propose a small improvement to the community exchange programme. People have noticed an invitation with an unclear request, and a short trial could help us understand how often this problem occurs. We should ask regular users and people who have not used the service before to describe their experiences. Their comments may reveal details that a plan made in an office would miss.
For one month, staff could keep a simple record of participation, time spent and any difficulties reported. We should also explain the purpose of the trial in clear language so that residents know how to contribute. After the month, please publish a brief summary of both benefits and limits. The final decision should be based on what people actually experienced, with a date for checking the arrangement again.
Yours sincerely,
A resident
